title: Deep-sea bioluminescence
text: Many animals in the deep ocean produce their own light. This process, called bioluminescence, happens when a chemical reaction inside special cells releases energy as light. Most of this light is blue because blue light travels farthest through seawater. For example, the anglerfish uses a glowing lure to attract small prey toward its mouth. Other species flash suddenly to startle predators or to find mates in the dark. However, scientists still do not fully understand how other animals interpret many of these signals.

title: Octopus camouflage
text: Octopuses can change the color of their skin in less than a second. Their skin contains thousands of small cells filled with colored pigment. When tiny muscles around these cells stretch or relax, the visible color changes. Some octopuses can also raise small bumps to copy the texture of rocks or coral. For example, a resting octopus may become almost invisible against a sandy seabed. Interestingly, octopuses appear to be color blind, so researchers are still studying how they match their surroundings so well.

title: Mammal hibernation
text: Some mammals survive cold winters by entering a state called hibernation. During this period, their body temperature drops and their heart rate slows dramatically. As a result, they use much less energy than they would if they stayed active. Ground squirrels, for example, may breathe only a few times per minute while hibernating. They rely on fat stored during the summer and autumn to stay alive. However, hibernating animals still wake up briefly every few weeks, and scientists are not completely sure why.

title: Moon and ocean tides
text: Ocean tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon. The side of the Earth facing the Moon is pulled more strongly than the center of the planet. This difference creates a bulge of water, and another forms on the opposite side. As the Earth rotates, most coastlines pass through both bulges each day. Consequently, many places experience two high tides and two low tides daily. The Sun also affects tides, although its influence is less than half that of the Moon.

title: Sound in different materials
text: Sound travels as a wave of vibrations that passes from particle to particle. In air, the particles are far apart, so the vibrations move relatively slowly. In water, the particles are closer together, and sound travels about four times faster. Solids such as steel carry sound even more quickly. This is why a person can sometimes hear an approaching train through the rails before hearing it through the air. However, sound cannot travel at all through the empty space between planets.

title: How lightning forms
text: Lightning forms when electrical charges build up inside storm clouds. Strong air currents carry ice crystals and small pieces of hail up and down within the cloud. When these particles collide, they exchange electric charge. Lighter crystals usually become positive and rise to the top, while heavier particles become negative and gather near the bottom. Eventually, the difference in charge becomes so large that a sudden discharge occurs. However, most lightning flashes never reach the ground and stay inside the cloud.

title: Rainbow formation
text: A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through drops of water in the air. As light enters each drop, it bends and separates into different colors. The light then reflects off the back of the drop and bends again as it leaves. Because each color bends by a different amount, the colors spread out into a band. To see a rainbow, an observer must stand with the Sun behind them. However, no two people see the same rainbow, because each observer receives light from different drops.

title: Moving sand dunes
text: Sand dunes are not fixed features but slowly move across the landscape. Wind pushes grains of sand up the gentle slope on one side of the dune. When the grains reach the top, they fall down the steeper slope on the other side. Over time, this process causes the whole dune to travel in the direction of the wind. Some desert dunes can move several meters each year. However, plants can slow this movement because their roots hold the sand in place.

title: Limestone caves
text: Most large caves form in limestone, a rock that slowly dissolves in weak acid. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil, which makes it slightly acidic. As this water flows through cracks in the rock, it gradually widens them into tunnels. Over thousands of years, these tunnels can grow into huge underground rooms. Dripping water also leaves behind minerals that build stalactites on cave ceilings. However, this process is extremely slow, so damaged cave formations may take centuries to recover.

title: Honeybee waggle dance
text: Honeybees share information about food through a movement called the waggle dance. A bee that has found flowers returns to the hive and walks in a figure of eight. During the straight part of the dance, she shakes her body from side to side. The direction of this run shows the direction of the food relative to the Sun. The length of the run indicates the distance to the flowers. However, other bees must follow the dancer in the dark hive to receive the message.

title: Autumn leaf color
text: In autumn, the leaves of many trees change from green to yellow, orange, or red. Leaves look green in summer because they contain large amounts of chlorophyll. As days become shorter and cooler, trees stop producing this pigment. The yellow and orange pigments, which were present all along, then become visible. Red colors are different because many trees produce them new in autumn. For example, maples often turn red after sunny days and cool nights. However, a dry summer can make autumn colors less impressive.

title: Static electricity
text: Static electricity is the buildup of electric charge on the surface of objects. When two materials rub together, electrons can move from one material to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged, while the other becomes positive. For example, rubbing a balloon on your hair can make it stick to a wall. A small shock may also occur when you touch a metal handle after walking across a carpet. However, static effects are weaker on humid days because moisture helps charges escape.

title: The ozone layer
text: The ozone layer is a region of the upper atmosphere that absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. Ozone molecules are formed when sunlight splits ordinary oxygen molecules apart. Without this layer, more radiation would reach the surface and damage living cells. In the past century, certain chemicals used in refrigerators and spray cans began to destroy ozone. An international agreement later banned most of these chemicals. As a result, the layer is slowly recovering, although full recovery is expected to take several more decades.

title: Fat fuel for migration
text: Many small birds travel thousands of kilometers during their yearly migrations. Before leaving, they eat large amounts of food and store the extra energy as fat. Some songbirds nearly double their body weight in just a few weeks. This fat is a very efficient fuel because it contains more energy per gram than sugar or protein. During long flights over oceans or deserts, the birds gradually burn these reserves. However, they usually need to stop at rest areas along the way to feed again.

title: Why the sea is salty
text: Seawater is salty because rivers carry dissolved minerals from land into the ocean. Rain slowly breaks down rocks and releases small amounts of salt into streams. When ocean water evaporates, the water leaves but the salt stays behind. Over millions of years, this process has made the sea much saltier than rivers. Salinity is not the same everywhere, however. For example, the Red Sea is very salty because of strong evaporation, while seas near melting ice are much less salty.

title: Antibiotic resistance
text: Antibiotic resistance arises when bacteria evolve the capacity to survive drugs that previously eliminated them. Whenever an antibiotic is administered, susceptible cells are destroyed, whereas the rare mutants that tolerate it subsequently multiply. Consequently, the surviving population becomes predominantly resistant within relatively few generations. Moreover, bacteria can exchange resistance genes directly through small circular pieces of DNA called plasmids. This phenomenon has been documented extensively in hospitals, where antibiotics are used intensively. Nevertheless, careful prescribing and improved hygiene can substantially mitigate its spread.

title: Ocean acidification
text: The ocean absorbs roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide that human activities release into the atmosphere. Although this uptake moderates climate change, it simultaneously alters the chemistry of seawater. When carbon dioxide dissolves, it forms carbonic acid, which subsequently lowers the pH of the water. Consequently, fewer carbonate ions remain available for organisms that construct shells and skeletons. Laboratory experiments have demonstrated that the larvae of oysters and other shellfish are particularly vulnerable to these conditions. Nevertheless, some species appear capable of adapting, so the long term outcomes remain uncertain.

title: Thawing permafrost
text: Permafrost is ground that remains frozen for at least two consecutive years, and it underlies vast areas of the Arctic. Enormous quantities of organic material have been preserved within it because decomposition is negligible at freezing temperatures. As the climate warms, however, the upper layers are increasingly thawing. Microbes subsequently break down the exposed material and release carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere. Consequently, thawing permafrost could amplify the very warming that triggered it. Nevertheless, the magnitude of this feedback remains difficult to predict precisely.

title: Circadian rhythms
text: Most organisms possess an internal clock that regulates their activities over a cycle of approximately one day. In mammals, this circadian clock is predominantly controlled by a small cluster of neurons in the brain. Although the clock operates independently, it is continually adjusted by external signals, particularly daylight. When people travel rapidly across several time zones, their internal rhythms become misaligned with local time. This mismatch, commonly known as jet lag, can impair sleep, digestion, and concentration. However, the clock gradually resynchronizes, typically within several days.

title: Superconductivity
text: Certain materials lose all electrical resistance when they are cooled below a specific critical temperature. This phenomenon, known as superconductivity, was first observed in mercury cooled with liquid helium. Because no energy is dissipated as heat, an electric current can circulate indefinitely in a superconducting loop. Superconducting magnets are consequently employed in medical scanners and particle accelerators. However, most superconductors function only at extremely low temperatures, which necessitates expensive cooling systems. Researchers are therefore searching for materials that remain superconducting closer to room temperature.

title: Auroras and the solar wind
text: Auroras are luminous displays that appear predominantly in the night skies near the polar regions. They originate with the solar wind, a continuous stream of charged particles emitted by the Sun. When these particles reach the Earth, most are deflected by its magnetic field. Some, however, are guided toward the poles, where they collide with gases in the upper atmosphere. These collisions excite oxygen and nitrogen atoms, which subsequently release energy as visible light. During intense solar storms, auroras may occasionally be observed at much lower latitudes.

title: Zebra mussel invasion
text: Invasive species are organisms that spread aggressively after being introduced to ecosystems where they did not previously occur. Zebra mussels, for instance, were unintentionally carried across the ocean in the ballast water of cargo ships and released into the Great Lakes. Because they lacked natural predators, their populations expanded rapidly throughout the region. They filter enormous volumes of water, thereby depleting the plankton on which native species depend. They also clog water intake pipes, which has necessitated costly maintenance. Nevertheless, some fish have subsequently begun to consume them.

title: Lake eutrophication
text: Eutrophication occurs when a body of water becomes excessively enriched with nutrients, particularly nitrogen and phosphorus. These nutrients predominantly originate from agricultural fertilizers and untreated wastewater. In response, algae multiply rapidly and form dense blooms at the surface. When the algae subsequently die, bacteria decompose them and consume large quantities of dissolved oxygen. Consequently, fish and other aquatic animals may suffocate in areas with little oxygen. Reducing fertilizer runoff can mitigate the problem, although recovery may be delayed because nutrients accumulate in lake sediments.

title: Desert plant photosynthesis
text: Many desert plants have evolved a specialized form of photosynthesis that minimizes water loss. Ordinary plants open their stomata during the day to absorb carbon dioxide, but this also allows considerable evaporation. By contrast, cacti and similar species open their stomata predominantly at night, when temperatures are lower and the air is more humid. The carbon dioxide is stored as an organic acid and subsequently used for photosynthesis during daylight. Consequently, these plants conserve water remarkably efficiently. However, this strategy generally results in slower growth.

title: Life cycle of Sun-like stars
text: Stars like the Sun spend most of their lives fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. When the hydrogen in the core is eventually exhausted, the star expands into a red giant. Its outer layers are subsequently expelled into space, where they form a glowing shell of gas. The remaining core, which is extremely dense, becomes a white dwarf that gradually cools over billions of years. A teaspoon of its material would weigh several tons on Earth. Considerably more massive stars, however, end their lives in violent explosions called supernovae.

title: Hydrothermal vent communities
text: Hydrothermal vents are openings on the seafloor through which water heated by underlying magma is released. Until their discovery in the late twentieth century, scientists assumed that virtually all ecosystems depended on sunlight. However, the communities surrounding these vents are sustained predominantly by chemosynthesis. In this process, bacteria derive energy from chemical compounds such as hydrogen sulfide rather than from light. Giant tube worms, for example, harbor these bacteria inside their bodies and obtain nourishment from them. Nevertheless, such communities remain vulnerable because individual vents may become inactive within decades.

title: The dinosaur extinction
text: About sixty-six million years ago, a mass extinction eliminated roughly three quarters of all species on Earth. The prevailing explanation attributes this event to the impact of an enormous asteroid, which struck the region that is now southern Mexico. The collision presumably ejected vast quantities of dust and sulfur into the atmosphere, which subsequently blocked sunlight for months. Consequently, photosynthesis declined sharply and food chains collapsed. This hypothesis is supported by a thin layer of sediment enriched in iridium, an element rare in crustal rocks. Nevertheless, some researchers contend that volcanic eruptions also contributed.

title: How catalysts work
text: A catalyst is a substance that accelerates a chemical reaction without being permanently consumed. It functions by providing an alternative pathway that requires less activation energy. Consequently, more of the collisions between molecules produce a reaction. In automobiles, for instance, catalytic converters transform toxic exhaust gases into less harmful substances. Enzymes, which are biological catalysts, similarly enable reactions in living cells to proceed rapidly at body temperature. However, catalysts do not alter the final balance of a reversible reaction; they merely allow it to be reached more quickly.

title: Sea otters as keystone species
text: Some predators exert an influence on their ecosystems that is far greater than their abundance would suggest. Such animals are referred to as keystone species. Along northern Pacific coasts, sea otters feed extensively on sea urchins, which in turn graze on kelp. Where otters were eliminated by the fur trade, urchin populations increased dramatically and subsequently destroyed entire kelp forests. Conversely, when otters were reintroduced, the kelp gradually recovered. Nevertheless, the strength of this effect varies considerably from one location to another.

title: Thermohaline circulation
text: Deep ocean currents are driven predominantly by differences in water density rather than by wind. Density depends on both temperature and salinity, so cold, salty water tends to sink. Near the poles, surface water is cooled intensely and becomes saltier as sea ice forms. This dense water subsequently descends and flows slowly toward the equator along the ocean floor. The resulting global circulation, known as the thermohaline circulation, redistributes heat between the tropics and the poles. However, scientists warn that a large influx of fresh meltwater could weaken this system.
